204	 Early Detection
205	 Athletic trainers and team physicians are in ideal positions to aid in the early detection
206	 of alcohol misuse. Proximity to, and time around athletes allows for frequent informal
207	 assessments and opportunities to learn about potential risky behaviors. Common
208	 behavioral signs of alcohol misuse that can be detected by athletic trainers, team phy-
209	 sicians, and other support staff are detailed in Table 1.
210	 Any athlete suspected of misusing alcohol or who has an adverse alcohol-related
211	 event (eg, blackout, fight, arrest, driving under the influence) should be assessed by
212	 the team physician or licensed mental health provider using motivational interviewing
213	 techniques and should receive the full 10-item Alcohol Use Disorders Inventory Test
214	 (AUDIT) adapted for use in the United States (USAAUDIT)40,41 and the 24 item Brief
215	 Young Adult Alcohol Consequences Questionnaire.42 USAAUDIT scores of 7 to 15
216	 for women and 8 to 15 for men indicate hazardous drinking and should result in feed-
217	 back and a brief intervention designed to reduce consumption and curb the adverse
218	 effects of alcohol misuse.
219	 Another early detection strategy is to include alcohol urine testing as part of the
220	 panel for random screening of drugs of abuse and performance enhancers. Any level
221	 of alcohol in a morning urine test indicates heavy drinking the night before and should
222	 be assessed via motivational interviewing and administration of the USAAUDIT.
223	 Finally, because of the increasing likelihood of simultaneous use of alcohol and
224	 cannabis misuse, a cannabis use history (frequency, intensity, route of administration)
225	 and screening with the 8-item CUDIT-R or the 3-item CUDIT-SF (see Appendix 3)
226	 should occur. If SAM is present, there is an increased risk for comorbid mental health
227	 diagnoses and a screening for anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder Screen-GAD-7),
228	 depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-PHQ-9), and sleep problems (Athlete Sleep
229	 Screening Questionnaire-ASSQ) should also be considered.26
230	 Brief Interventions
231	 Psychoeducation about the adverse effects of alcohol on sleep, energy, reaction time,
232	 emotional control, interpersonal relationships, and injury risk as well as its likelihood of
233	 reducing athletic and academic performance is a primary component of brief interven-
234	 tion strategies for alcohol misuse. Many athletes are unaware of the fixed metabolism
235	 of alcohol (only one drink an hour) which makes it unique among substances of misuse
236	 and increases the risk of heavy, rapid drinking. In addition, if alcohol is used simulta-
237	 neously with cannabis or sedative/anxiety/depression medications (prescribed or over
238	 the counter) such as antihistamines, benzodiazepines, selective serotonin reuptake in-
239	 hibitors (SSRIs), or sleeping pills, this potentiates the intoxicating effects of alcohol
240	 and makes adverse effects more likely.1,2,4 Providing athletes with this information
241	 can help them make more educated decisions about their alcohol consumption.
242	 For more serious alcohol misuse, as evidenced by a score of 16 to 24 on the
243	 USAAUDIT, a series of 1 to 4 brief motivational interviewing sessions should be imple-
244	 mented by a mental health provider working directly with the athlete/team or by an
245	 outpatient substance treatment program. These sessions should include personalized
246	 feedback, social norming, goal setting (academic, athletic, social), involvement of sig-
247	 nificant others (eg, peer, parent, coach), strategies for cutting down aimed at changing
248	 patterns of harmful use, and/or a trial of abstinence.
249	 One example of such an intervention was created by Donohue and colleagues32 for
250	 incoming first-year collegiate athletes. Following an assessment of the athletes’ drink-
251	 ing behaviors, they created a one-session model (individual or group) with a follow-up
252	 assessment at 2 months that was led by a performance coach and included significant

272	CANNABIS
273	Background
274	Self-reported rates of cannabis (marijuana) use and misuse among US collegiate and
275	professional athletes are rising due to its expanded availability from medicalization/
276	legalization and the decision by some professional sports (eg, Major League Baseball,
277	National Football League) to reduce or discontinue random urine testing and eliminate
278	sanctions in favor of evaluation and treatment.10–12,16,44,45 Sports medicine providers
279	should be aware of the prevalence rates, reasons for use, patterns of use, adverse ef-
280	fects, trends in potency, signs of misuse, and detection and intervention strategies for
281	this substance.2,4,6,16
282	 Studies of elite athletes in general show that approximately 1 in 4 use
283	cannabis.10,16,44 In US collegiate athletes, annual use rates are higher in: (1) men
284	than women (26.3% vs 22.3%); (2) lacrosse, swimming, and wrestling for men
285	(50%, 35%, 29% respectively), (3) lacrosse, ice hockey, field hockey, soccer and
286	volleyball for women (34%, 29%, 29%, 27%, 27% respectively), (4) Division III than Di-
287	vision I (33% vs 18%) and in (5) states where it is legal than in those where it is not
288	(39% vs 26%).16 The most common reasons for use are socialization, pain control,
289	well-being, stress reduction, and insomnia.16,44
290	 Patterns of use range from episodic cannabidiol (CBD) alone and/or delta 9 tetrahy-
291	drocannabinol (THC with CBD simultaneously) to long-term regular use of higher po-
292	tency THC with or without CBD and/or simultaneous use of alcohol and marijuana.25,44
293	The most common routes of administration are inhaling (eg, smoking, vaping) or inges-
294	tion (edibles, tinctures)16 and the most common short-term adverse behavioral effects
295	are detailed in Tables 1.46–48 When cannabis use becomes daily or near daily, the risk
296	of additional adverse effects including the use of other illicit substances (eg, cocaine,
297	methamphetamine), motor vehicle accidents, athletic injuries, permanent cognitive
298	impairment, reduced life achievement, psychosis and/or progression to a cannabis
299	use disorder becomes more likely.46–50 In general, 1 out of 9 cannabis users progress
300	to a use disorder; however, this increases to 1 in 6 if use starts in adolescence and to 1
301	in 4 for those that use daily.46 Many of these adverse effects are due to the potency
302	(THC level) of herbal US cannabis products which has risen over the past decade
303	from approximately 10% in 2009 to 14% in 2019.51 Similar increases have occurred
304	in the United Kingdom, Central Europe, and New Zealand.52 Cannabis levels are

308	 highest in cannabis concentrates (eg, ear wax, hash oil) with THC levels of 40% to

311	 Early Detection
312	 Annual preseason psychoeducational presentations on the patterns, prevalence, po-
313	 tency, and adverse effects of cannabis use and misuse to groups of athletes or teams
314	 with the distribution of a companion fact sheet or negative consequences question-
315	 naire may prompt individuals to ask more questions about their use and review the
316	 pros and cons of continuing. Athletic trainers, team physicians, and sports mental
317	 health and performance providers should be educated regarding cannabis’ early
318	 behavioral effects and typical signs and symptoms of intoxication and withdrawal
319	 (see Table 1).54,55
320	 Random or surveillance urine testing is another way of identifying cannabis users or
321	 misusers. Random testing refers to testing small groups of athletes on a team each
322	 week with the intention of testing all team members over the season or the year. Sur-
323	 veillance testing refers to testing all members (or a representative sample – 50%) with
324	 or without the results being connected to a specific athlete’s name to determine the
325	 point prevalence of use. This might be done for sports that are known to have the high-
326	 est rates of use (eg, lacrosse, swimming, ice hockey, field hockey). High individual
327	 urine levels (ie, above 150 ng/mL) may indicate a daily or near daily user and warrant
328	 an evaluation.
329	 Screening instruments such as the four question Cutting Down, Annoyance by Crit-
330	 icism, Guilty Feelings, Eye-opener modified to include cannabis/marijuana (CAGE-
331	 AID)26 or the three question Cannabis Use Disorder Screening Tool-Short-Form
332	 (CUDIT-SF) which uses questions 3, 5, and 6 of the longer CUDIT-R27 are recommen-
333	 ded to identify misuse (see Appendices 2 and 3). A score of 2 or more indicates a pos-
334	 itive screen for both the CAGE-AID and CUDIT-SF. A positive screen on one or both
335	 should result in a clinical assessment with a team physician or licensed mental health
336	 provider along with the administration of the 20-item Brief Marijuana Consequences
337	 Questionnaire.30
338	 Brief Interventions
339	 The literature on brief motivational interventions with personalized feedback for
340	 cannabis use and misuse in elite athletes is scarce. Like college students, young adult
341	 athletes at collegiate and professional levels are increasingly viewing cannabis use as
342	 safe and socially acceptable with a companion view that much higher percentages of
343	 their teammates are using than actually are.24,25,56,57
344	 Given the documented adverse effects of both regular alcohol and cannabis use in
345	 athletes (see Table 1), brief interventions conducted by athletic trainers, team physi-
346	 cians, and/or sports mental health and substance providers are warranted.24,50
347	 There is some evidence that brief motivational interventions with personalized feed-
348	 back compared to assessment without intervention or psychoeducation alone can
349	 reduce positive expectancies and frequency of use, change attitudes about cannabis’
350	 safety and levels of normative use, and potentially prevent adverse consequences in
351	 non-athlete samples of adolescents and college students.58–60 These motivational in-
352	 terventions are typically designed to encourage participants to change their behavior,
353	 teach behavioral coping and change skills, and connect to services using the FRAMES
354	 model (ie,; personalized feedback, reinforcement of personal responsibility, non-
355	 judgmental advice, menu of strategies, empathetic listening, and activation of self-
356	 efficacy).56

364	2-h training module with content on patterns and prevalence of use, risks for
365	alcohol-related injury, risks for alcohol and cannabis-related academic difficulties,
366	and skill building for motivational interviewing. The skill-building section of the module
367	was designed to teach athletic personnel to have “meaningful conversations” about
368	student athlete use and facilitate guiding help-seeking behaviors.
369	 Another intervention mentioned earlier by Rulison and colleagues (2022)34 used an
370	iteratively modified version of myPlaybook during three trials of approximately 2000 to
371	3000 each Division I, II, and III athletes with content on norms of alcohol and cannabis
372	use, expectancies of drug effects, harm reduction and life skills. For cannabis, they

375	 Finally, an alternative approach by Lee and colleagues (2021)59 developed a novel

377	attempted to more accurately document the common consequences of cannabis

380	(83.9%); (2) experienced dry mouth (3) had trouble concentrating or paying attention

382	(57.4%); and (6) had low motivation (46.4%). They suggest using the MCC to generate
383	a motivational discussion and deliver personalized feedback based on the response
384	patterns from the 336 undergraduates that completed the checklist.
385	 Based on the available evidence, coaches, athletic trainers, team physicians, and/or
386	on-site mental health or substance use providers can use team-based presentations
387	to present information on the adverse effects of cannabis use alone or in combination
388	with alcohol and administer either the Brief Marijuana Consequences Questionnaire30
389	or the Marijuana Consequences Checklist.61 Those with regular or heavy patterns of
390	cannabis use and a higher number of negative consequences can then receive individ-
391	ual personalized feedback with an open motivational discussion of the potential nega-
392	tive effects of cannabis on athletic and academic performance. Those who continue
393	the use/misuse after this “open discussion” should have a formal assessment by a
394	mental health provider and potential referral to an outpatient treatment program.

400	lacrosse.16,62 Overall annual use rates of the various tobacco products and nicotine

405	lacrosse (35%) and wrestling (33%) and high rates for cigarettes in lacrosse (38%),
406	golf (23%) and ice hockey (23%). Overall annual use rates for women collegiate ath-
407	letes are far lower than for men for both cigarettes (5.3% vs 14%) and oral tobacco
408	(0.6% vs 21.8%). However, just as for men, women’s use rates vary significantly by

438	 Early Detection
439	 Awareness of the high prevalence of tobacco use and nicotine vaping in certain sports
440	 (eg, ice hockey, baseball, American football, wrestling, golf) is one key to early detec-
441	 tion. Questions about tobacco use and nicotine vaping should be included in the
442	 pre-season physical examination along with alcohol and cannabis. If use is endorsed,
443	 then additional screening with the 6-question Fagerstrom Dependence Scale (FDS -
444	 Appendix 4) should be considered.66 A score of 5 or more indicates a significant
445	 dependence, while a score of 4 or less shows a low to moderate dependence. An
446	 additional approach is to have the team dentist do an oral exam at the time of the pre-
447	 season physical examination looking for signs of gum irritation or oral lesions (ie, leu-
448	 koplakia). If the exam is positive, then more questions about the current and past
449	 pattern of use and desire to quit should be asked.
450	 Brief Interventions
451	 There are no recent studies of brief interventions for elite athletes who are using or
452	 misusing tobacco products or vaping nicotine. Older studies from 1999 to 2003 in
453	 high school, collegiate, and professional baseball players (where oral tobacco use
454	 rates in minor league and major league players ranged from 25% to 35%) have
455	 demonstrated the effectiveness of brief interventions in increasing the perception of
456	 risk and reducing levels of use.67–70 Most of these studies included a dentist or dental
457	 assistant led, peer assisted brief intervention that occurred at the time of the presea-
458	 son physical exam. The intervention provided personalized feedback regarding cur-
459	 rent, or future, oral health problems, level of nicotine dependence using the FDS,
460	 and provided strategies for quitting. In some of these dental-based interventions,

480	REFERRAL TO TREATMENT
481	When an athlete is not responding to the brief intervention strategies described above,
482	or is diagnosed as having a substance use disorder, they may benefit from referral to
483	an addiction specialist for a more comprehensive evaluation to determine the next
484	steps. Alternatively, if the athlete is already demonstrating medical signs and symp-
485	toms of withdrawal that indicate pending instability (ie, alcohol withdrawal-Table 1),
486	they may require immediate medical detoxification in an outpatient or inpatient setting.
487	 Treatment for a substance use disorder exists on a spectrum with the American So-
488	ciety of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) identifying 5 benchmark levels of care as a method
489	of standardizing addiction treatment80. Level 0/0.5 includes prevention and early inter-
490	vention and includes brief intervention strategies discussed above. Outpatient ser-
491	vices are the focus of Level 1, while Level 2 is comprised of intensive outpatient
492	and partial hospitalization services. Level 3 involves residential/inpatient services
493	including clinically managed low-intensity and high-intensity residential services,
494	and medically monitored intensive inpatient services. Level 4 is the highest level of
495	care and is comprised of medically managed intensive inpatient services.72
496	 The topical areas explored in the criteria for determining the appropriate level of care
497	include (but are not limited to) medical complexity, behavioral health complexity, read-
498	iness to change, environmental instability, and previous experience in treatment set-
499	tings. The process of determining the level of care and criterion match is best
500	executed by a trained clinician and is typically completed upon initial intake and evalu-
501	ation to a new treatment facility. Based upon this clinical assessment, the client enters
502	treatment at a certain level best matched to address their level of instability and need,
503	with the goal to progress to less clinically rigorous engagement as their needs evolve.
504	Not every program is able to satisfy the definition of the full spectrum and may offer
505	alternative referral if the individual demonstrates needs greater than what is available.
506	DISCUSSION
507	Sports medicine physicians and athletic trainers are in prime positions to help with the
508	early identification, assessment, and brief intervention for substance misuse and
509	abuse among athletes. Knowing utilization and misuse patterns of the sport you are
510	working with can help enhance awareness of symptoms guide best questions to
511	ask. Across all sports and competition levels, the most encountered substances of

515	 misuse are alcohol (binge drinking), cannabis (marijuana), and nicotine (oral tobacco/
516	 nicotine vaping). While more detailed data exists for the collegiate population, there is
517	 limited data among professional athletes, especially current professional athletes in
518	 the US, making it more challenging to know prevalence rates for this population.
519	 Continued exploration of use and misuse patterns along with adverse consequences
520	 of use will help develop more effective prevention, assessment, and intervention pro-
521	 cesses for this population.
522	 Development of an organizational plan for training, identification, intervention, and
523	 treatment prior to the start of the season will help sports medicine staff know when
524	 and how to assess for misuse of alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine. Pre-participation
525	 physicals is an ideal time for sports medicine staff to begin asking questions and
526	 assessing behaviors via self-report screeners, open-ended questioning, medical
527	 exams, and urine screens. Following transitions and acute events (ie, injury, trade,
528	 transfer, and so forth) is another time to screen for changes in behaviors and sub-
529	 stance use patterns. While discrete transitions provide ideal times for screening,
530	 sports medicine staff have frequent interactions and access to players that allows
531	 for ongoing informal screening and behavior monitoring throughout the year.
532	 While geared toward sports medicine physicians and athletic trainers, many other
533	 athlete-facing staff may be in roles to help facilitate prevention, identification, and early
534	 intervention depending on the organization and individual athlete relationships.
535	 Coaches, player engagement/development staff, dieticians, strength and condition-
536	 ing, and equipment staff are a few of the groups that may be in positions to identify
537	 signs and symptoms of misuse/abuse. Training with all athlete-facing staff can help
538	 with identification and referral to the sports medicine staff for further assessment
539	 and evaluation when warranted.
540	 Training for sports medicine staff on early identification, motivational interviewing,
541	 and brief interventions for alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine use is recommended. Part-
542	 nering with licensed mental health providers can aid in this training and provide an
543	 easy transition from brief intervention to higher levels of ongoing care. The ASAM
544	 levels of care outline the continuum of treatment based on patterns of use and symp-
545	 toms. It is important for sports medicine staff to develop relationships with addiction
546	 specialists in the community along with local area treatment facilities providing the full
547	 spectrum of care. These relationships will help facilitate access to, and transition of
548	 care when higher levels of treatment is warranted.
549	 CLINICS CARE POINTS
550	  Screening for alcohol, cannabis, and tobacco/nicotine misuse prior to each season can lead to
551	 early detection and brief intervention.
552	  The simultaneous use of alcohol with either cannabis or tobacco/nicotine is associated with
553	 increased adverse effects.
554	  Brief Motivational Intervention training for substance misuse should become a part of the
555	 ongoing education of athletic trainers and team physicians.

Early Detection, Brief Intervention and Referral
to Treatment
David R. McDuff, MDa,b,c,*, Michelle Garvin, PhDd,e,
Joy Chang, MDa,f, Donald Thompson, MDa,b
 KEYWORDS
  Substance misuse  Alcohol  Cannabis  Tobacco  Nicotine  Elite athletes
  Early detection
 KEY POINTS
  Encounters with alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine/tobacco misuse is common.
  Early identification can reduce the negative consequences of misuse and prevent the pro-
 gression to a substance use disorder.
  The use of screening instruments, negative consequences questionnaires, and urine
 testing can aid early identification.
  Brief motivational interventions with personalized feedback, social norming, goal setting,
 contingency management, and significant other involvement can change attitudes, be-
 liefs, and use patterns.
  The simultaneous use of alcohol and marijuana (SAM) among athletes is increasing and is
 associated with increased adverse effects.
 The authors declare no commercial or financial conflicts of interest and no funding sources
 were associated with this work.

 2 McDuff et al
 INTRODUCTION
 Sports medicine physicians and athletic trainers regularly encounter athletes who
 misuse substances that put them at risk for adverse social, interpersonal, academic,
 psychological, health and performance effects.1–6 The most often encountered sub-
 stances in collegiate and professional athletes are alcohol (binge drinking), cannabis
 (marijuana), and nicotine (oral tobacco/nicotine vaping).7–15 Male athletes typically
 misuse substances at higher rates than female athletes and male and female athletes
 from certain sports (eg, lacrosse, ice hockey, swimming, rugby) have the highest rates
 of use and misuse.16–19 Differences in use and misuse rates of some substances in
 athletes versus non-athletes can begin in high school where, for example, binge drink-
 ing rates for athletes is higher than in non-athletes by 9th grade.8
 Alcohol and other substance use typically begins as recreational or social use in
 high school and increases from 8th to 12th grades in both athlete and general student
 populations.19,20 In 2022 a national survey demonstrated that past year use rates were
 significantly higher for 12th graders than 8th graders for alcohol (51.9% vs 15.2%),
 cannabis (30.7% vs 8.3%), and nicotine vaping (27.3% vs 12%). For some athletes,
 substance use becomes more regular and heavier, progressing to misuse by the
 end of high school. Misuse is defined as using alcohol or other drugs in a manner, sit-
 uation, amount, or frequency that could cause harm to a user or to those around
 them.21 Common adverse effects vary somewhat by substance class, but include
 physical, social, legal, emotional, performance and academic consequences2,11,16
 (Table 1). If substance misuse is identified early, prompt intervention can prevent pro-
 gression to a substance disorder with or without comorbid mental health symptoms
 and disorders.
 Substances may be used individually or concurrently with an increasing trend for us-
 ing two together such that their psychogenic and behavioral effects overlap. The
 simultaneous use of alcohol and marijuana (SAM) and alcohol and tobacco/nicotine
 is common among college students including student athletes.22–25 When two sub-
 stances are used simultaneously, additive adverse effects such as heavier and
 more frequent use, driving while impaired, academic and athletic underperformance,
 and an increased probability of developing comorbid substance use and mental health
 disorders are likely.23

 in combination, is critical to prevent the range of negative consequences and/or pro-

 urine testing are important mitigation strategies.1,2,4 Given the amount of time that
 sports medicine physicians and athletic trainers spend with athletes, they are in the

 Once alcohol, cannabis, and/or nicotine/tobacco misuse is identified and an in-
depth assessment has been conducted, various interventions such as psychoeduca-
tion, direct or web-based individualized feedback, goal setting, support system
involvement, contingency management and/or brief motivational interventions can
be considered.31–34 If these interventions are not effective in reducing substance
use and/or its adverse effects, then referral to more targeted treatment (eg, outpatient,
intensive outpatient, residential, inpatient detoxification) may be necessary.
 This article will focus on alcohol, cannabis, and tobacco misuse and explore early
detection, brief interventions, and referral to treatment. Additionally, a brief description
of the available levels of care for the treatment of severe or intractable substance
misuse or a substance use disorder will be presented.
ALCOHOL
Background
Binge drinking, with a range of adverse effects, is commonly encountered in US col-
legiate and professional athletes with certain sports (eg, lacrosse, rugby, ice hockey,
swimming, baseball, field hockey) exhibiting higher rates than the general population.
Binge drinking is defined as 4 or more standard drinks per drinking occasion for fe-
males and 5 or more drinks for males. Super binge drinking is defined as 10 or
more drinks per drinking occasion and is seen more often in US male collegiate ath-
letes (13%) than in female collegiate athletes (1.8%). Binge and super binge drinking
are typically defined by the presence of one or more binge drinking episodes over the
past two weeks.16 For male collegiate athletes, certain sports have high rates for
binge drinking ranging from 50% for wrestling to 64% and 69% for ice hockey and
lacrosse respectively. For females, the sports with the highest rates range from
43% for volleyball to 56% and 57% for ice hockey and lacrosse respectively.16 The
most endorsed negative effects for binge drinking among collegiate athletes are
hangover (52%), loss of memory of events (28.4%), regret of behaviors (25.4%), inter-
rupted/lost sleep (20.7%), got into an argument or a fight (16.8%) and missed a class
(14.2%).16 Even though binge drinking rates for US collegiate athletes from all sports
have declined from 2009 to 2017 (58% to 44% for men; 51% to 39% for women), the
rates are still high in certain sports and the adverse consequences are serious (ie,
physical injury (6.8%), poor academic performance (7.1%), and/or poor athletic per-
formance (7.4%)).16
 Very limited data exist on the rates of alcohol misuse (including heavy use and
binge drinking) among current professional athletes, especially in the US. The
data that exists from Europe and Australasia suggests that in general, rates of
alcohol misuse are highly variable depending on the sport.18,35–39 For example, a
study of professional soccer players from five European countries found rates of
current alcohol misuse that ranged from 6.0% in Sweden to 15.7% and 17% for
Spain and Finland, respectively.35 A study of professional rugby players from Aus-
tralasian countries ranged from 22% misuse rates in one study36 to much higher
rates of 62.8% in another.37 Rates among current and retired professional ice
hockey players from four European countries were 7.6% for current players and
28.7% for retired ones.38 Somewhat higher current rates were seen in active pro-
fessional cricket players from South Africa (26%), while retired professional crick-
eters had rates of 22%.39 Both of these studies included male athletes only.
However, a study of male and female professional soccer players in Australia found
the rate of alcohol misuse in the women athletes (43.8%) to be lower than that of
males (50.7%).18

 Early Detection
 Athletic trainers and team physicians are in ideal positions to aid in the early detection
 of alcohol misuse. Proximity to, and time around athletes allows for frequent informal
 assessments and opportunities to learn about potential risky behaviors. Common
 behavioral signs of alcohol misuse that can be detected by athletic trainers, team phy-
 sicians, and other support staff are detailed in Table 1.
 Any athlete suspected of misusing alcohol or who has an adverse alcohol-related
 event (eg, blackout, fight, arrest, driving under the influence) should be assessed by
 the team physician or licensed mental health provider using motivational interviewing
 techniques and should receive the full 10-item Alcohol Use Disorders Inventory Test
 (AUDIT) adapted for use in the United States (USAAUDIT)40,41 and the 24 item Brief
 Young Adult Alcohol Consequences Questionnaire.42 USAAUDIT scores of 7 to 15
 for women and 8 to 15 for men indicate hazardous drinking and should result in feed-
 back and a brief intervention designed to reduce consumption and curb the adverse
 effects of alcohol misuse.
 Another early detection strategy is to include alcohol urine testing as part of the
 panel for random screening of drugs of abuse and performance enhancers. Any level
 of alcohol in a morning urine test indicates heavy drinking the night before and should
 be assessed via motivational interviewing and administration of the USAAUDIT.
 Finally, because of the increasing likelihood of simultaneous use of alcohol and
 cannabis misuse, a cannabis use history (frequency, intensity, route of administration)
 and screening with the 8-item CUDIT-R or the 3-item CUDIT-SF (see Appendix 3)
 should occur. If SAM is present, there is an increased risk for comorbid mental health
 diagnoses and a screening for anxiety (Generalized Anxiety Disorder Screen-GAD-7),
 depression (Patient Health Questionnaire-PHQ-9), and sleep problems (Athlete Sleep
 Screening Questionnaire-ASSQ) should also be considered.26
 Brief Interventions
 Psychoeducation about the adverse effects of alcohol on sleep, energy, reaction time,
 emotional control, interpersonal relationships, and injury risk as well as its likelihood of
 reducing athletic and academic performance is a primary component of brief interven-
 tion strategies for alcohol misuse. Many athletes are unaware of the fixed metabolism
 of alcohol (only one drink an hour) which makes it unique among substances of misuse
 and increases the risk of heavy, rapid drinking. In addition, if alcohol is used simulta-
 neously with cannabis or sedative/anxiety/depression medications (prescribed or over
 the counter) such as antihistamines, benzodiazepines, selective serotonin reuptake in-
 hibitors (SSRIs), or sleeping pills, this potentiates the intoxicating effects of alcohol
 and makes adverse effects more likely.1,2,4 Providing athletes with this information
 can help them make more educated decisions about their alcohol consumption.
 For more serious alcohol misuse, as evidenced by a score of 16 to 24 on the
 USAAUDIT, a series of 1 to 4 brief motivational interviewing sessions should be imple-
 mented by a mental health provider working directly with the athlete/team or by an
 outpatient substance treatment program. These sessions should include personalized
 feedback, social norming, goal setting (academic, athletic, social), involvement of sig-
 nificant others (eg, peer, parent, coach), strategies for cutting down aimed at changing
 patterns of harmful use, and/or a trial of abstinence.
 One example of such an intervention was created by Donohue and colleagues32 for
 incoming first-year collegiate athletes. Following an assessment of the athletes’ drink-
 ing behaviors, they created a one-session model (individual or group) with a follow-up
 assessment at 2 months that was led by a performance coach and included significant

fewer athletes use substances regularly), positive alcohol expectancies (reduced),

CANNABIS
Background
Self-reported rates of cannabis (marijuana) use and misuse among US collegiate and
professional athletes are rising due to its expanded availability from medicalization/
legalization and the decision by some professional sports (eg, Major League Baseball,
National Football League) to reduce or discontinue random urine testing and eliminate
sanctions in favor of evaluation and treatment.10–12,16,44,45 Sports medicine providers
should be aware of the prevalence rates, reasons for use, patterns of use, adverse ef-
fects, trends in potency, signs of misuse, and detection and intervention strategies for
this substance.2,4,6,16
 Studies of elite athletes in general show that approximately 1 in 4 use
cannabis.10,16,44 In US collegiate athletes, annual use rates are higher in: (1) men
than women (26.3% vs 22.3%); (2) lacrosse, swimming, and wrestling for men
(50%, 35%, 29% respectively), (3) lacrosse, ice hockey, field hockey, soccer and
volleyball for women (34%, 29%, 29%, 27%, 27% respectively), (4) Division III than Di-
vision I (33% vs 18%) and in (5) states where it is legal than in those where it is not
(39% vs 26%).16 The most common reasons for use are socialization, pain control,
well-being, stress reduction, and insomnia.16,44
 Patterns of use range from episodic cannabidiol (CBD) alone and/or delta 9 tetrahy-
drocannabinol (THC with CBD simultaneously) to long-term regular use of higher po-
tency THC with or without CBD and/or simultaneous use of alcohol and marijuana.25,44
The most common routes of administration are inhaling (eg, smoking, vaping) or inges-
tion (edibles, tinctures)16 and the most common short-term adverse behavioral effects
are detailed in Tables 1.46–48 When cannabis use becomes daily or near daily, the risk
of additional adverse effects including the use of other illicit substances (eg, cocaine,
methamphetamine), motor vehicle accidents, athletic injuries, permanent cognitive
impairment, reduced life achievement, psychosis and/or progression to a cannabis
use disorder becomes more likely.46–50 In general, 1 out of 9 cannabis users progress
to a use disorder; however, this increases to 1 in 6 if use starts in adolescence and to 1
in 4 for those that use daily.46 Many of these adverse effects are due to the potency
(THC level) of herbal US cannabis products which has risen over the past decade
from approximately 10% in 2009 to 14% in 2019.51 Similar increases have occurred
in the United Kingdom, Central Europe, and New Zealand.52 Cannabis levels are

 Early Detection
 Annual preseason psychoeducational presentations on the patterns, prevalence, po-
 tency, and adverse effects of cannabis use and misuse to groups of athletes or teams
 with the distribution of a companion fact sheet or negative consequences question-
 naire may prompt individuals to ask more questions about their use and review the
 pros and cons of continuing. Athletic trainers, team physicians, and sports mental
 health and performance providers should be educated regarding cannabis’ early
 behavioral effects and typical signs and symptoms of intoxication and withdrawal
 (see Table 1).54,55
 Random or surveillance urine testing is another way of identifying cannabis users or
 misusers. Random testing refers to testing small groups of athletes on a team each
 week with the intention of testing all team members over the season or the year. Sur-
 veillance testing refers to testing all members (or a representative sample – 50%) with
 or without the results being connected to a specific athlete’s name to determine the
 point prevalence of use. This might be done for sports that are known to have the high-
 est rates of use (eg, lacrosse, swimming, ice hockey, field hockey). High individual
 urine levels (ie, above 150 ng/mL) may indicate a daily or near daily user and warrant
 an evaluation.
 Screening instruments such as the four question Cutting Down, Annoyance by Crit-
 icism, Guilty Feelings, Eye-opener modified to include cannabis/marijuana (CAGE-
 AID)26 or the three question Cannabis Use Disorder Screening Tool-Short-Form
 (CUDIT-SF) which uses questions 3, 5, and 6 of the longer CUDIT-R27 are recommen-
 ded to identify misuse (see Appendices 2 and 3). A score of 2 or more indicates a pos-
 itive screen for both the CAGE-AID and CUDIT-SF. A positive screen on one or both
 should result in a clinical assessment with a team physician or licensed mental health
 provider along with the administration of the 20-item Brief Marijuana Consequences
 Questionnaire.30
 Brief Interventions
 The literature on brief motivational interventions with personalized feedback for
 cannabis use and misuse in elite athletes is scarce. Like college students, young adult
 athletes at collegiate and professional levels are increasingly viewing cannabis use as
 safe and socially acceptable with a companion view that much higher percentages of
 their teammates are using than actually are.24,25,56,57
 Given the documented adverse effects of both regular alcohol and cannabis use in
 athletes (see Table 1), brief interventions conducted by athletic trainers, team physi-
 cians, and/or sports mental health and substance providers are warranted.24,50
 There is some evidence that brief motivational interventions with personalized feed-
 back compared to assessment without intervention or psychoeducation alone can
 reduce positive expectancies and frequency of use, change attitudes about cannabis’
 safety and levels of normative use, and potentially prevent adverse consequences in
 non-athlete samples of adolescents and college students.58–60 These motivational in-
 terventions are typically designed to encourage participants to change their behavior,
 teach behavioral coping and change skills, and connect to services using the FRAMES
 model (ie,; personalized feedback, reinforcement of personal responsibility, non-
 judgmental advice, menu of strategies, empathetic listening, and activation of self-
 efficacy).56

increased education and brief intervention skill development for athletic personnel
(eg, coaches, athletic trainers, strength and conditioning staff).24 They developed a
2-h training module with content on patterns and prevalence of use, risks for
alcohol-related injury, risks for alcohol and cannabis-related academic difficulties,
and skill building for motivational interviewing. The skill-building section of the module
was designed to teach athletic personnel to have “meaningful conversations” about
student athlete use and facilitate guiding help-seeking behaviors.
 Another intervention mentioned earlier by Rulison and colleagues (2022)34 used an
iteratively modified version of myPlaybook during three trials of approximately 2000 to
3000 each Division I, II, and III athletes with content on norms of alcohol and cannabis

attempted to more accurately document the common consequences of cannabis
use of typical users. They discovered that for monthly or more frequent users, the
top 6 “not so good” consequences over the past 30 days were: (1) had the munchies
(83.9%); (2) experienced dry mouth (3) had trouble concentrating or paying attention
(62.5%); (4) acted foolish or goofy (61.9%); (5) had trouble remembering things
(57.4%); and (6) had low motivation (46.4%). They suggest using the MCC to generate
a motivational discussion and deliver personalized feedback based on the response
patterns from the 336 undergraduates that completed the checklist.
 Based on the available evidence, coaches, athletic trainers, team physicians, and/or
on-site mental health or substance use providers can use team-based presentations
to present information on the adverse effects of cannabis use alone or in combination
with alcohol and administer either the Brief Marijuana Consequences Questionnaire30
or the Marijuana Consequences Checklist.61 Those with regular or heavy patterns of
cannabis use and a higher number of negative consequences can then receive individ-

the use/misuse after this “open discussion” should have a formal assessment by a
mental health provider and potential referral to an outpatient treatment program.
TOBACCO/NICOTINE
Background
The use and misuse of oral (spit) tobacco and other tobacco products (eg, cigars, cig-
arettes, hookah) and/or nicotine vaping is regularly encountered by sports medicine
providers especially those that work in baseball, hockey, wrestling, golf, and
lacrosse.16,62 Overall annual use rates of the various tobacco products and nicotine
vaping for US male collegiate athletes are: oral tobacco (21.8%); cigars (17%); ciga-
rettes (14%); hookah (10%); and electronic cigarettes (8%) with 5% reporting daily
use of oral tobacco.16 There is substantial variation in annual male use rates by sports
with far higher rates for annual oral tobacco use in ice hockey (46%), baseball (44%),
lacrosse (35%) and wrestling (33%) and high rates for cigarettes in lacrosse (38%),
golf (23%) and ice hockey (23%). Overall annual use rates for women collegiate ath-
letes are far lower than for men for both cigarettes (5.3% vs 14%) and oral tobacco
(0.6% vs 21.8%). However, just as for men, women’s use rates vary significantly by

 Early Detection
 Awareness of the high prevalence of tobacco use and nicotine vaping in certain sports
 (eg, ice hockey, baseball, American football, wrestling, golf) is one key to early detec-
 tion. Questions about tobacco use and nicotine vaping should be included in the
 pre-season physical examination along with alcohol and cannabis. If use is endorsed,
 then additional screening with the 6-question Fagerstrom Dependence Scale (FDS -
 Appendix 4) should be considered.66 A score of 5 or more indicates a significant
 dependence, while a score of 4 or less shows a low to moderate dependence. An
 additional approach is to have the team dentist do an oral exam at the time of the pre-
 season physical examination looking for signs of gum irritation or oral lesions (ie, leu-
 koplakia). If the exam is positive, then more questions about the current and past
 pattern of use and desire to quit should be asked.

 There are no recent studies of brief interventions for elite athletes who are using or
 misusing tobacco products or vaping nicotine. Older studies from 1999 to 2003 in

 risk and reducing levels of use.67–70 Most of these studies included a dentist or dental
 assistant led, peer assisted brief intervention that occurred at the time of the presea-
 son physical exam. The intervention provided personalized feedback regarding cur-

REFERRAL TO TREATMENT
When an athlete is not responding to the brief intervention strategies described above,
or is diagnosed as having a substance use disorder, they may benefit from referral to
an addiction specialist for a more comprehensive evaluation to determine the next
steps. Alternatively, if the athlete is already demonstrating medical signs and symp-
toms of withdrawal that indicate pending instability (ie, alcohol withdrawal-Table 1),
they may require immediate medical detoxification in an outpatient or inpatient setting.
 Treatment for a substance use disorder exists on a spectrum with the American So-
ciety of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) identifying 5 benchmark levels of care as a method
of standardizing addiction treatment80. Level 0/0.5 includes prevention and early inter-
vention and includes brief intervention strategies discussed above. Outpatient ser-
vices are the focus of Level 1, while Level 2 is comprised of intensive outpatient
and partial hospitalization services. Level 3 involves residential/inpatient services
including clinically managed low-intensity and high-intensity residential services,
and medically monitored intensive inpatient services. Level 4 is the highest level of
care and is comprised of medically managed intensive inpatient services.72
 The topical areas explored in the criteria for determining the appropriate level of care
include (but are not limited to) medical complexity, behavioral health complexity, read-
iness to change, environmental instability, and previous experience in treatment set-
tings. The process of determining the level of care and criterion match is best
executed by a trained clinician and is typically completed upon initial intake and evalu-
ation to a new treatment facility. Based upon this clinical assessment, the client enters
treatment at a certain level best matched to address their level of instability and need,
with the goal to progress to less clinically rigorous engagement as their needs evolve.
Not every program is able to satisfy the definition of the full spectrum and may offer
alternative referral if the individual demonstrates needs greater than what is available.
DISCUSSION
Sports medicine physicians and athletic trainers are in prime positions to help with the
early identification, assessment, and brief intervention for substance misuse and
abuse among athletes. Knowing utilization and misuse patterns of the sport you are
working with can help enhance awareness of symptoms guide best questions to
ask. Across all sports and competition levels, the most encountered substances of

 Development of an organizational plan for training, identification, intervention, and
 treatment prior to the start of the season will help sports medicine staff know when
 and how to assess for misuse of alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine. Pre-participation
 physicals is an ideal time for sports medicine staff to begin asking questions and
 assessing behaviors via self-report screeners, open-ended questioning, medical
 exams, and urine screens. Following transitions and acute events (ie, injury, trade,
 transfer, and so forth) is another time to screen for changes in behaviors and sub-
 stance use patterns. While discrete transitions provide ideal times for screening,
 sports medicine staff have frequent interactions and access to players that allows
 for ongoing informal screening and behavior monitoring throughout the year.
 While geared toward sports medicine physicians and athletic trainers, many other
 athlete-facing staff may be in roles to help facilitate prevention, identification, and early
 intervention depending on the organization and individual athlete relationships.
 Coaches, player engagement/development staff, dieticians, strength and condition-
 ing, and equipment staff are a few of the groups that may be in positions to identify
 signs and symptoms of misuse/abuse. Training with all athlete-facing staff can help
 with identification and referral to the sports medicine staff for further assessment
 and evaluation when warranted.
 Training for sports medicine staff on early identification, motivational interviewing,
 and brief interventions for alcohol, cannabis, and nicotine use is recommended. Part-
 nering with licensed mental health providers can aid in this training and provide an
 easy transition from brief intervention to higher levels of ongoing care. The ASAM
 levels of care outline the continuum of treatment based on patterns of use and symp-
 toms. It is important for sports medicine staff to develop relationships with addiction
 specialists in the community along with local area treatment facilities providing the full
 spectrum of care. These relationships will help facilitate access to, and transition of
 care when higher levels of treatment is warranted.
 CLINICS CARE POINTS
  Screening for alcohol, cannabis, and tobacco/nicotine misuse prior to each season can lead to
 early detection and brief intervention.
  The simultaneous use of alcohol with either cannabis or tobacco/nicotine is associated with
 increased adverse effects.
  Brief Motivational Intervention training for substance misuse should become a part of the
 ongoing education of athletic trainers and team physicians.

 "evidenceSummary": "A systematic review (PubMed, Embase and Web of Science searched to September 2018) of 27 studies using ultrasound tissue characterization (UTC) of Achilles (18 studies), patellar (5) or both (4) tendons. Samples were mostly small cohorts of athletes and recreational or sedentary participants with and without tendinopathy, and the authors judged methods too heterogeneous to pool.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review is narrative and descriptive, with no formal quality appraisal and no pooled analysis, and most studies came from a small group of authors. Evidence on patellar tendinopathy is thin, and the search ended in September 2018, so later UTC studies are not included.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read UTC as a validated tool for predicting or managing tendinopathy, but the authors found the predictive evidence inconclusive, reported no clear link between echo-type changes and symptoms, and noted UTC has been validated for equine rather than human tendon.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2021,
  "citation": "Rabello LM, Dams OC, van den Akker-Scheek I, Zwerver J, O'Neill S. Substantiating the Use of Ultrasound Tissue Characterization in the Analysis of Tendon Structure: A Systematic Review. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(3):e161-e175.",
  "doi": "10.1097/JSM.0000000000000749",
  "abstract": "The authors reviewed 27 studies to determine how ultrasound tissue characterization (UTC) can predict, diagnose and monitor tendon structure and tendinopathy, and to propose a standard scanning and analysis method. UTC was a possible adjunct for diagnosing Achilles tendinopathy and showed promise for monitoring load and treatment, but its predictive value was inconclusive.",
  "tldr": "Ultrasound tissue characterization may help show tendon changes in response to load or treatment and can add diagnostic information in Achilles tendinopathy. It has not been shown to predict who will develop tendinopathy, and scanning methods still need to be standardised before results can be compared.",
  "methods": "Systematic review following PRISMA guidance, with two reviewers screening in three rounds (titles and abstracts, then full text) and a third reviewer resolving disagreements. Data were extracted on design, participants, scanning method (position, scan direction, window size, area analysed) and whether UTC was used to predict, diagnose or monitor tendons. The review was narrative and descriptive, with no quality assessment or pooled analysis.",
  "findings": "Of 27 included studies, 18 examined the Achilles tendon, 5 the patellar tendon and 4 both. Predictive studies gave inconsistent results for Achilles tendinopathy, while a higher percentage of disorganised tissue (echo types III and IV) was linked to patellar tendinopathy in one study. For diagnosis, UTC separated symptomatic from asymptomatic Achilles tendons in some studies (one reported 83% accuracy). For monitoring, several studies showed changes in echo types after loading or treatment, although results varied across studies. Scanning methods differed widely across studies.",
  "limitations": "No formal quality assessment and no pooled analysis because the studies were heterogeneous in design, population and method. Most studies focused on mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, and patellar tendon evidence is limited. Few diagnostic studies exist and there is no gold-standard reference for echo types. The search closed in September 2018 and several authors contributed multiple studies.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use UTC as an adjunct to clinical assessment and conventional imaging, not as the sole basis for predicting tendinopathy. If UTC is used to track tendon response to load, use the same standardised method each time (position, scan direction, window size 9 or 17, contours no more than 5 mm apart) and compare repeat scans in the same way.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Consider UTC scans to track how Achilles or patellar tendons adapt to a loading block, using the same protocol each time. Do not use echo-type changes alone to decide how much load an athlete can take, since the link to symptoms is unclear.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: UTC may help monitor tendon structure during rehabilitation, but the review found no clear link between echo-type changes and clinical outcome, so it cannot be used alone to decide when an athlete is ready to return to sport."
 }

  "Mixed / General Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Injured Athletes",
  "Mixed / Unspecified"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "A systematic review (PubMed, Embase and Web of Science searched to September 2018) of 27 studies using ultrasound tissue characterization (UTC) of Achilles (18 studies), patellar (5) or both (4) tendons. Samples were mostly small cohorts of athletes and recreational or sedentary participants with and without tendinopathy, and the authors judged methods too heterogeneous to pool.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review is narrative and descriptive, with no formal quality appraisal and no pooled analysis, and most studies came from a small group of authors. Evidence on patellar tendinopathy is thin, and the search ended in September 2018, so later UTC studies are not included.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read UTC as a validated tool for predicting or managing tendinopathy, but the authors found the predictive evidence inconclusive, reported no clear link between echo-type changes and symptoms, and noted UTC has been validated for equine rather than human tendon.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2021,
  "citation": "Rabello LM, Dams OC, van den Akker-Scheek I, Zwerver J, O'Neill S. Substantiating the Use of Ultrasound Tissue Characterization in the Analysis of Tendon Structure: A Systematic Review. Clin J Sport Med. 2021;31(3):e161-e175.",
  "doi": "10.1097/JSM.0000000000000749",
  "abstract": "The authors reviewed 27 studies to determine how ultrasound tissue characterization (UTC) can predict, diagnose and monitor tendon structure and tendinopathy, and to propose a standard scanning and analysis method. UTC was a possible adjunct for diagnosing Achilles tendinopathy and showed promise for monitoring load and treatment, but its predictive value was inconclusive.",
  "tldr": "Ultrasound tissue characterization may help show tendon changes in response to load or treatment and can add diagnostic information in Achilles tendinopathy. It has not been shown to predict who will develop tendinopathy, and scanning methods still need to be standardised before results can be compared.",
  "methods": "Systematic review following PRISMA guidance, with two reviewers screening in three rounds (titles and abstracts, then full text) and a third reviewer resolving disagreements. Data were extracted on design, participants, scanning method (position, scan direction, window size, area analysed) and whether UTC was used to predict, diagnose or monitor tendons. The review was narrative and descriptive, with no quality assessment or pooled analysis.",
  "findings": "Of 27 included studies, 18 examined the Achilles tendon, 5 the patellar tendon and 4 both. Predictive studies gave inconsistent results for Achilles tendinopathy, while a higher percentage of disorganised tissue (echo types III and IV) was linked to patellar tendinopathy in one study. For diagnosis, UTC separated symptomatic from asymptomatic Achilles tendons in some studies (one reported 83% accuracy). For monitoring, several studies showed changes in echo types after loading or treatment, although results varied across studies. Scanning methods differed widely across studies.",
  "limitations": "No formal quality assessment and no pooled analysis because the studies were heterogeneous in design, population and method. Most studies focused on mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, and patellar tendon evidence is limited. Few diagnostic studies exist and there is no gold-standard reference for echo types. The search closed in September 2018 and several authors contributed multiple studies.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use UTC as an adjunct to clinical assessment and conventional imaging, not as the sole basis for predicting tendinopathy. If UTC is used to track tendon response to load, use the same standardised method each time (position, scan direction, window size 9 or 17, contours no more than 5 mm apart) and compare repeat scans in the same way.",

14	 analysis differed and were not uniform. The studies showed that the use of UTC to predict Achilles tendinopathy (AT) is inconclusive,

18	 predicting tendon pathology is required. Ultrasound tissue characterization seems useful as an adjunct diagnostic modality be-

General Review
Substantiating the Use of Ultrasound Tissue
Characterization in the Analysis of Tendon
Structure: A Systematic Review
Lucas Maciel Rabello, MSc,* Olivier Christian Dams, BSc,* Inge van den Akker-Scheek, PhD,*†
Johannes Zwerver, PhD,* and Seth O’Neill, PhD‡
 Abstract
 Objective: To determine the role of ultrasound tissue characterization (UTC) in predicting, diagnosing, and monitoring tendon
 structure and/or tendinopathy. In addition, this study aims to provide recommendations for standardized methodology of UTC
 administration and analysis. Data Source: The PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science databases were searched (up to
 September 2018). All scientific literature concerning the use of UTC in assessing tendons was collected. The initial search resulted in
 a total of 1972 hits, and after screening by eligibility criteria, 27 articles were included. Results: In total, 18 investigating the Achilles
 tendon, 5 the patellar tendon, and 4 both Achilles and patellar tendons were included. The methods of UTC administration and
 analysis differed and were not uniform. The studies showed that the use of UTC to predict Achilles tendinopathy (AT) is inconclusive,
 but that a higher amount of tendon disorganization increases the risk of developing patellar tendinopathy (PT). In terms of diagnosis,
 UTC might provide additional information in AT cases. In addition, promising results were found for the use of UTC in both AT and PT
 in monitoring the effect of load or treatment on tendon structure. Conclusion: More research regarding the use of UTC in
 predicting tendon pathology is required. Ultrasound tissue characterization seems useful as an adjunct diagnostic modality be-
 cause it can be used to differentiate symptomatic from asymptomatic tendons. In addition, UTC is a promising device to be used to
 monitor changes in tendon structure in response to load or treatment. Moreover, we provide recommendations of a standardized
 protocol concerning the methods of UTC measurement and analysis.
 Key Words: tendinopathy, ultrasound, Achilles tendon, patellar tendon

 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "A systematic review and meta-cluster analysis of 22 studies (5,592 athletes with sport-related concussion) searched in Medline, Embase, PsycINFO and SPORTDiscus up to December 2018. Multiple correspondence analysis of the reported symptom clusters identified five clusters (migraine, cognitive-emotional, sleep-emotional, neurological and undefined feelings), and 19 studies linked these clusters to clinical outcomes, most often longer recovery.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Most included studies had limitations, and only 13.6% used exploratory data-driven clustering, so analysis bias may have shaped the clusters. The clusters were derived from published reports rather than individual data, the included athletes were mostly adolescents, and the review does not show that subtype-specific treatment improves recovery.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could treat the five clusters as proven concussion subtypes that should drive treatment choice; the authors say subtype-targeted management is untested and that it is unclear which clusters relate to specific functional impairments.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2020,
  "citation": "Langdon S, Königs M, Adang EAM, Goedhart E, Oosterlaan J. Subtypes of Sport-Related Concussion: a Systematic Review and Meta-cluster Analysis. Sports Med. 2020.",
  "doi": "10.1007/s40279-020-01321-9",
  "abstract": "The authors systematically reviewed 22 studies of sport-related concussion symptom clusters and their links to clinical outcome, aggregating the cluster findings with multiple correspondence analysis. They identified five symptom clusters, with the migraine cluster most often reported and most strongly linked to outcome.",
  "tldr": "Concussion symptoms appear to group into about five clusters, and the migraine-type cluster is the one most closely tied to longer recovery. Clinicians may use these groupings to think about symptom profiles, but treatment decisions based on them still need testing.",
  "methods": "Systematic review following MOOSE guidance, searching four databases from 1946 to December 2018 for studies that identified symptom clusters or linked clusters to outcomes after sport-related concussion. Two reviewers screened and extracted data, and risk of bias was assessed with an adapted Cochrane tool. Reported clusters were pooled with multiple correspondence analysis, and cluster-outcome links were summarised with effect sizes where available.",
  "findings": "Of 22 included studies (5,592 athletes), six found symptom clusters and 19 linked clusters to outcomes. The meta-analysis identified a migraine cluster (headache, light and noise sensitivity, nausea), a cognitive-emotional cluster, a sleep-emotional cluster, a neurological cluster (blurred vision, vomiting, neck pain) and an undefined feelings cluster. Migraine-type clusters were most frequently reported (24%) and linked to prolonged symptom duration and cognitive, balance and oculomotor deficits, with the largest effect sizes. The undefined feelings cluster was not linked to any outcome.",
  "limitations": "Most included studies had methodological limitations, and only 13.6% used exploratory data-driven clustering. Clusters were pooled from published reports rather than individual data, and the athletes were mostly adolescents. The authors note that the included studies did not consistently adjust for age, sex and time since injury. Whether particular clusters relate to specific functional impairments remains unclear.",
  "practicalImplications": "Record symptom profiles in the first week after concussion, paying particular attention to headache, light and noise sensitivity, sleep and emotional symptoms, since these clusters were most linked to slower recovery. Use the profile to guide assessment, such as headache, cognitive, sleep and vestibular checks, rather than assuming one management pathway for all athletes.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: This review does not address training or performance directly. Its relevance is to recognising concussion profiles and to communicating with athletes about symptom patterns that predict a slower return to training.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Symptom clusters, especially the migraine-type cluster, were linked to prolonged recovery and symptom duration, so they may help flag athletes who need a longer, more cautious return. The review does not show that cluster-based management shortens return to sport, and it cannot set return-to-play timelines."
 }
}

Subtypes of Sport‑Related Concussion: a Systematic Review
and Meta‑cluster Analysis
S. Langdon1,2 · M. Königs1,2 · E. A. M. C. Adang1 · E. Goedhart2 · J. Oosterlaan1
© The Author(s) 2020
Abstract
Objective Current clinical guidelines provide a unitary approach to manage sport-related concussion (SRC), while hetero-
geneity in the presentation of symptoms suggests that subtypes of SRC may exist. We systematically reviewed the available
evidence on SRC subtypes and associated clinical outcomes.
Data Sources Ovid Medline, Embase, PsycINFO, and SPORTDiscus
Eligibility Criteria for Selecting Studies Electronic databases were searched for studies: (i) identifying SRC symptom clusters
using classification methodology; or (ii) associating symptom clusters to clinical outcome variables. A total of 6,146 unique
studies were identified, of which 75 full texts were independently assessed by two authors for eligibility. A total of 22 articles
were included for systematic review.
Data Extraction Two independent authors performed data extraction and risk of bias analysis using the Cochrane Collabora-
tion tool.
Data Synthesis Six studies found evidence for existence of SRC symptom clusters. Combining the available literature through
Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA) provided evidence for the existence of a migraine cluster, a cognitive–emotional
cluster, a sleep–emotional cluster, a neurological cluster, and an undefined feelings cluster. Nineteen studies found meaning-
ful associations between SRC symptom clusters and clinical outcomes. Clusters mapping to the migraine cluster were most
frequently reported in the literature and were most strongly related to aspects of clinical outcome.
Conclusions The available literature provides evidence for the existence of at least five subtypes in SRC symptomatology,
with clear relevance to clinical outcome. Systematically embedding the differentiation of SRC subtypes into prognosis,
clinical management, and intervention strategies may optimize the recovery from SRC.

{
 "id": "Q30",
 "sourceFile": "Sudden cardiac death in young athletes - JACC State of the Art Review.pdf",
 "decision": "INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason": "",
 "degradedReason": "",
 "doiMissing": false,
 "identityCheck": "Title in text 'Sudden Cardiac Death in Young Athletes: JACC State-of-the-Art Review' matches the filename.",
 "confidence": "high",
 "studyDesign": "Narrative Review",
 "primaryDomain": "Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains": [
  "Sports Medicine & Injury",
  "Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"
 ],
 "audiences": [
  "Sports Medicine",
  "Athletic Training",
  "Coaching"
 ],
 "sports": [
  "Mixed / General Sport"
 ],
 "populations": [
  "Youth / Adolescent",
  "Collegiate",
  "Professional / Elite"
 ],
 "evidenceSummary": "A state-of-the-art review in JACC (2024) of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, drawing on registries, autopsy series and national databases from the United States, Italy, the United Kingdom, Israel and Denmark. It summarises the causes (inherited cardiomyopathies, channelopathies and coronary anomalies), diagnostic overlap with the athlete's heart, screening and resuscitation, and shared decision making on exercise after cardiac disease. No systematic search method is described.",
 "screeningLimitations": "The review has no described search method, so the evidence base cannot be reproduced. Reported incidence varies widely across cohorts because of differing definitions (sudden cardiac death or arrest), age ranges and case ascertainment, and many autopsy rates are low. Much of the guidance on exercise after cardiac disease rests on retrospective or observational data.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the review as showing that most athletes with a cardiac diagnosis can keep training at high intensity, but the authors stress that intensity and volume effects are not well established and that decisions should follow individual expert assessment.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,
  "citation": "Finocchiaro G, Westaby J, Sheppard MN, Papadakis M, Sharma S. Sudden Cardiac Death in Young Athletes: JACC State-of-the-Art Review. J Am Coll Cardiol. 2024;83(2):350-370.",
  "doi": "10.1016/j.jacc.2023.10.032",
  "abstract": "This state-of-the-art review covers the epidemiology and causes of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, including cardiomyopathies, channelopathies and coronary anomalies. It also addresses the difficulty of separating the athlete's heart from disease, preparticipation screening, resuscitation, and shared decision making about exercise when a cardiac condition is found.",
  "tldr": "Sudden cardiac death in young athletes is rare but usually linked to an inherited heart condition or coronary anomaly that was not detected beforehand. A cardiac diagnosis does not automatically end sport, and decisions should follow expert assessment and shared decision making.",
  "methods": "Narrative state-of-the-art review. No systematic search method is described. The authors draw on incidence studies, national registries, autopsy series and guideline statements from the United States, Europe and elsewhere, and summarise Table 2 comparing AHA/ACC and ESC recommendations for sports participation.",
  "findings": "Reported incidence of sudden cardiac death in young athletes varies widely, from 0.24 per 100,000 athlete-years in Minnesota high school athletes to 6.8 per 100,000 athlete-years in a screened UK adolescent football cohort. Inherited cardiomyopathies and coronary anomalies are the most common causes, with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and coronary anomalies all reported. Athlete's heart changes can overlap with cardiomyopathy and channelopathy findings, and the review describes ECG and imaging features that help separate them. Compulsory screening in Veneto, Italy, was linked to an 89% fall in incidence in one account, while a study in Israel found no reduction. The review also notes that recent guidelines take a more liberal, shared decision making approach to exercise in several cardiac conditions.",
  "limitations": "No search method is described, and the review relies on heterogeneous definitions and case ascertainment. The authors note that autopsy rates are declining and that some cohorts underestimate events. Evidence on the effects of intense exercise in people with cardiac disease is mainly from retrospective or observational studies, and the authors call for randomised trials.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use a holistic assessment combining personal and family history, ECG and imaging before clearing an athlete, and recognise that many cardiac findings are physiological. Keep resuscitation readiness high, with trained staff, a plan and access to an automated external defibrillator, and discuss exercise limits with the athlete and team physician when a condition is found.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Keep athletes' cardiac screening, emergency action plans and defibrillator access in place through the season. When an athlete has an unusual ECG or heart scan, check with the team physician before increasing training intensity.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review gives guideline-based guidance on sports participation after a cardiac diagnosis, such as cardiomyopathy or channelopathy, and recommends shared decision making. It does not provide a return-to-play protocol after cardiac arrest, and the authors note the evidence on high-intensity exercise is limited."
 }
}

  "doi": "10.1016/j.jacc.2023.10.032",
  "abstract": "This state-of-the-art review covers the epidemiology and causes of sudden cardiac death in young athletes, including cardiomyopathies, channelopathies and coronary anomalies. It also addresses the difficulty of separating the athlete's heart from disease, preparticipation screening, resuscitation, and shared decision making about exercise when a cardiac condition is found.",
  "tldr": "Sudden cardiac death in young athletes is rare but usually linked to an inherited heart condition or coronary anomaly that was not detected beforehand. A cardiac diagnosis does not automatically end sport, and decisions should follow expert assessment and shared decision making.",
  "methods": "Narrative state-of-the-art review. No systematic search method is described. The authors draw on incidence studies, national registries, autopsy series and guideline statements from the United States, Europe and elsewhere, and summarise Table 2 comparing AHA/ACC and ESC recommendations for sports participation.",
  "findings": "Reported incidence of sudden cardiac death in young athletes varies widely, from 0.24 per 100,000 athlete-years in Minnesota high school athletes to 6.8 per 100,000 athlete-years in a screened UK adolescent football cohort. Inherited cardiomyopathies and coronary anomalies are the most common causes, with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy and coronary anomalies all reported. Athlete's heart changes can overlap with cardiomyopathy and channelopathy findings, and the review describes ECG and imaging features that help separate them. Compulsory screening in Veneto, Italy, was linked to an 89% fall in incidence in one account, while a study in Israel found no reduction. The review also notes that recent guidelines take a more liberal, shared decision making approach to exercise in several cardiac conditions.",
  "limitations": "No search method is described, and the review relies on heterogeneous definitions and case ascertainment. The authors note that autopsy rates are declining and that some cohorts underestimate events. Evidence on the effects of intense exercise in people with cardiac disease is mainly from retrospective or observational studies, and the authors call for randomised trials.",
  "practicalImplications": "Use a holistic assessment combining personal and family history, ECG and imaging before clearing an athlete, and recognise that many cardiac findings are physiological. Keep resuscitation readiness high, with trained staff, a plan and access to an automated external defibrillator, and discuss exercise limits with the athlete and team physician when a condition is found.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Keep athletes' cardiac screening, emergency action plans and defibrillator access in place through the season. When an athlete has an unusual ECG or heart scan, check with the team physician before increasing training intensity.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The review gives guideline-based guidance on sports participation after a cardiac diagnosis, such as cardiomyopathy or channelopathy, and recommends shared decision making. It does not provide a return-to-play protocol after cardiac arrest, and the authors note the evidence on high-intensity exercise is limited."

 Sudden Cardiac Death in Young Athletes
 JACC State-of-the-Art Review
 Gherardo Finocchiaro, MD, PHD, Joseph Westaby, PHD, BMBS, Mary N. Sheppard, MD, MBBCH, BAO, BSC,
 Michael Papadakis, MD, MBBS, Sanjay Sharma, MD, BSC(HONS)
 ABSTRACT
 Athletes epitomize the healthiest segment of society. Despite this premise, sudden cardiac death may occur in apparently
 healthy athletes, attracting signiﬁcant attention not only in the medical community but also in laypersons and media. The
 incidence of sudden cardiac death is variably reported, and epidemiological burden differs among cohorts. Athletes
 appear to be at risk of developing fatal arrhythmias when harboring a quiescent cardiac disorder. Primary cardiomyop-
 athies, ion channelopathies, and coronary artery anomalies are prevalent causes in young individuals. Cardiac assessment
 of athletes can be challenging because these individuals exhibit a plethora of electrical, structural, and functional
 physiological changes that overlap with cardiac pathology. A diagnosis of cardiac disease in a young athlete is not
 necessarily an indication to terminate competition and sports participation. International guidelines, traditionally focused
 on disqualiﬁcation of individuals with cardiac disease, have recently adopted a more liberal attitude, based on a careful
 assessment of the risk and on a shared-decision making approach. (J Am Coll Cardiol 2024;83:350–370)

 preexercise food-sourced calcium intake on acute bone metabolism in response to exercise? This article describes the content of
