 "evidenceSummary": "A descriptive epidemiology study combining NFL Injury Surveillance System records from 2000 to 2014 with the NFL Scouting Combine medical records of 2,965 athletes from 2003 to 2011. SLAP tears were 3.1% (65) of NFL shoulder injuries, most often in offensive linemen, and surgically treated tears missed more days (140.2 vs 21.5) and games (8.4 vs 2.6) than nonoperative ones. Of 25 Combine athletes with a prior SLAP repair, those drafted (n = 18) played fewer games (33.7 vs 48.3, P = .049) and started fewer (19.6 vs 35.4, P = .036) than 18 matched drafted controls.",
 "screeningLimitations": "Small numbers (65 in-game and practice SLAP tears, 25 Combine athletes, 18 matched pairs), self-reported Combine history that likely underestimates the true rate, and a surveillance system that did not record SLAP subtype, severity or surgical detail. Days missed included estimated return dates, and the authors are employed by a firm that consults for the NFL, so the analysis used league-funded data.",
 "synthesisCaution": "Staff could read the surgery-related time loss as a direct effect of surgery; the authors say injury severity is a likely confounder that the data cannot separate, and the career differences come from a small matched sample.",
 "paper": {
  "year": 2017,
  "citation": "Chambers CC, Lynch TS, Gibbs DB, Ghodasra JH, Sahota S, Franke K, et al. Superior Labrum Anterior-Posterior Tears in the National Football League. Am J Sports Med. 2017;45(1):167.",
  "doi": "10.1177/0363546516673350",
  "abstract": "The authors analysed SLAP tears in NFL players using league injury surveillance data from 2000 to 2014 and Scouting Combine records from 2003 to 2011. SLAP tears were a small share of shoulder injuries, surgically treated tears caused much more time lost, and Combine athletes with prior repair who were drafted had fewer games played and started.",
  "tldr": "SLAP tears are uncommon in NFL players but cost substantial time when they need surgery. Players with a prior SLAP repair who were drafted played noticeably fewer games than matched peers.",
  "methods": "Two-part descriptive study. NFL Injury Surveillance System records of SLAP tears from 2000 to 2014 were analysed by position, play type, days and games lost and surgery. Scouting Combine athletes from 2003 to 2011 with a prior SLAP repair were identified from medical evaluations and compared with matched drafted controls on career length and performance score. Groups were compared with t tests and chi-square tests.",
  "findings": "SLAP tears were 3.1% of NFL shoulder injuries (65 cases), most often in offensive linemen (27.7%), and about two-thirds occurred in games. Surgical treatment (41.5% of cases) was associated with more days missed (140.2 vs 21.5, P < .001) and games missed (8.4 vs 2.6, P = .003) than nonoperative care. Of 2,965 Combine athletes, 25 reported a prior SLAP repair; 18 of them were drafted, and compared with 18 matched controls they had similar performance scores (3.63 for both) and years played (3.4 vs 4.0, P = .063), but fewer games played (33.7 vs 48.3, P = .049) and games started (19.6 vs 35.4, P = .036).",
  "limitations": "Small sample sizes and possible underreporting of less severe injuries, particularly in Combine self-reported history. The surveillance system did not record SLAP subtype, injury severity or surgical detail, so the time-loss comparison may reflect severity. Estimated return dates were included in days missed, and career statistics came partly from public sources. The authors call for confirmation in larger populations.",
  "practicalImplications": "Treat a SLAP tear in a contact athlete as a potentially career-affecting injury and plan for substantial time lost if surgery is needed. Most in-game SLAP tears occurred during contact plays, mainly tackling and blocking, so the mechanism and play type are worth recording when a contact athlete presents with shoulder symptoms. The study did not test any prevention or treatment strategy.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Track shoulder history at the Combine and in medical screening, since prior SLAP repair was linked to fewer games played and started. Plan load and contact exposure carefully for linemen returning from shoulder injury.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: Surgically treated SLAP tears in NFL players were followed by a mean of 140 days missed compared with about three weeks for nonoperative management, which gives a rough time-loss benchmark. The study does not measure return to prior performance level after surgery, so it cannot guide return-to-play criteria."
 }
}

8	Background: Shoulder disorders are common in football players, with up to 50% of National Football League (NFL) recruits re-
9	porting a history of shoulder injuries. Superior labrum anterior-posterior (SLAP) tears are an entity with well-described detrimental
10	effects on return to play in overhead-throwing athletes but with minimal data in contact athletes.
11	Purpose: To identify the incidence, predisposing factors, and effect of SLAP tears in NFL athletes and prospects as well as the
12	treatment patterns of NFL team physicians.
13	Study Design: Descriptive epidemiology study.
14	Methods: This study was a comprehensive analysis of SLAP tears in elite football players using a dual approach: (1) SLAP injuries
15	recorded in the NFL Injury Surveillance System from 2000 to 2014 were evaluated by player position, type of play, days/games
16	lost, and surgical intervention; (2) NFL Scouting Combine athletes from 2003 to 2011 with prior SLAP repair were evaluated for
17	draft success, and drafted athletes were compared with matched controls for career length and performance scores.
18	Results: SLAP tears represented a small portion (3.1%) of shoulder injuries in NFL athletes from 2000 to 2014, occurring most
19	commonly in offensive linemen (28%). Surgically treated SLAP tears (42%) resulted in more days missed than did nonoperatively
20	managed tears (140.2 vs 21.5 days; P \ .001) and more games missed (8.4 vs 2.6 games; P = .003). SLAP repairs were also rare
21	in NFL Combine athletes (n = 25 of 2965 athletes), with most having been performed in offensive linemen (32%). As compared
22	with control NFL Combine athletes without SLAP tears, those drafted into the NFL with prior SLAP repair played significantly
23	fewer games (33.7 vs 48.3; P = .049) and had fewer game starts (19.6 vs 35.4; P = .036).
24	Conclusion: In this comprehensive analysis of SLAP tears in elite football players, it is clear that these injuries have the potential

Tears in the National Football League
Caitlin C. Chambers,*y MD, ATC, T. Sean Lynch,z MD, Daniel B. Gibbs,y MD,
Jason H. Ghodasra,§ MD, Shawn Sahota,y MD, Kristina Franke,|| MPH,
Christina D. Mack,|| PhD, and Gordon W. Nuber,{ MD
Investigation performed at Northwestern University and at NorthShore University, Chicago,
Illinois, USA
Background: Shoulder disorders are common in football players, with up to 50% of National Football League (NFL) recruits re-
porting a history of shoulder injuries. Superior labrum anterior-posterior (SLAP) tears are an entity with well-described detrimental
effects on return to play in overhead-throwing athletes but with minimal data in contact athletes.
Purpose: To identify the incidence, predisposing factors, and effect of SLAP tears in NFL athletes and prospects as well as the
treatment patterns of NFL team physicians.
Study Design: Descriptive epidemiology study.
Methods: This study was a comprehensive analysis of SLAP tears in elite football players using a dual approach: (1) SLAP injuries
recorded in the NFL Injury Surveillance System from 2000 to 2014 were evaluated by player position, type of play, days/games
lost, and surgical intervention; (2) NFL Scouting Combine athletes from 2003 to 2011 with prior SLAP repair were evaluated for
draft success, and drafted athletes were compared with matched controls for career length and performance scores.
Results: SLAP tears represented a small portion (3.1%) of shoulder injuries in NFL athletes from 2000 to 2014, occurring most
commonly in offensive linemen (28%). Surgically treated SLAP tears (42%) resulted in more days missed than did nonoperatively
managed tears (140.2 vs 21.5 days; P \ .001) and more games missed (8.4 vs 2.6 games; P = .003). SLAP repairs were also rare
in NFL Combine athletes (n = 25 of 2965 athletes), with most having been performed in offensive linemen (32%). As compared
with control NFL Combine athletes without SLAP tears, those drafted into the NFL with prior SLAP repair played significantly
fewer games (33.7 vs 48.3; P = .049) and had fewer game starts (19.6 vs 35.4; P = .036).
Conclusion: In this comprehensive analysis of SLAP tears in elite football players, it is clear that these injuries have the potential
to cause significant detriment to an athlete’s career.
